Reading 1: The Paradox of Technological Progress
Technological progress is frequently associated with increased efficiency, convenience, and economic development. Over the past few decades, digital innovations have transformed industries, facilitated communication, and provided individuals with unprecedented access to information. Nevertheless, the relationship between technological advancement and human well-being is considerably more complicated than it initially appears.
One apparent paradox is that technologies designed to save time often create additional demands on people’s attention. Smartphones, for instance, enable employees to communicate instantly, regardless of their physical location. However, this convenience can gradually undermine the distinction between professional responsibilities and personal life. Rather than reducing workloads, digital connectivity sometimes extends working hours and creates an expectation of constant availability.
Another concern involves the growing dependence on automated systems. Although automation can eliminate repetitive tasks and improve accuracy, excessive reliance on technology may weaken certain human capabilities. When individuals routinely delegate decisions to algorithms, they may become less inclined to question the assumptions underlying automated recommendations.
Furthermore, technological benefits are not distributed equally. Individuals with limited digital literacy or inadequate access to reliable infrastructure may struggle to participate fully in an increasingly digital economy. Consequently, innovation can unintentionally reinforce existing social inequalities.
This does not imply that technological development should be restricted. Instead, policymakers and businesses must recognize that efficiency is not the only measure of progress. Technological systems should be evaluated according to their broader social consequences, including their effects on autonomy, equality, and psychological well-being.
Ultimately, meaningful progress requires a balance between innovation and human interests. Technology should enhance people’s ability to make informed decisions rather than gradually replacing their capacity to do so.
Questions
	•	What paradox does the author identify regarding time-saving technologies?
	•	How can constant digital connectivity affect professional and personal boundaries?
	•	Why might excessive reliance on automated systems weaken human capabilities?
	•	How can technological innovation reinforce social inequality?
	•	What criteria, beyond efficiency, should be used to evaluate technological progress?
Reading 2: The Changing Nature of Education
Education has traditionally been regarded as a structured process through which individuals acquire knowledge and develop professional skills. For generations, formal qualifications were considered reliable indicators of competence and intellectual achievement. However, rapid changes in technology and employment patterns have challenged the assumption that education should primarily take place during the early stages of life.
One significant development is the growing recognition of lifelong learning. As industries evolve, professional knowledge can become outdated surprisingly quickly. Employees who wish to remain competitive must therefore continue developing their skills throughout their careers. This may involve attending professional courses, completing online programmes, or acquiring practical experience through independent projects.
Nevertheless, lifelong learning should not be reduced to a purely economic activity. Education also contributes to intellectual independence, cultural understanding, and critical thinking. Individuals who regularly encounter unfamiliar ideas may become more capable of evaluating information objectively and recognizing the limitations of their existing beliefs.
Another important issue is the changing relationship between qualifications and practical competence. Although academic degrees remain valuable in many professions, employers increasingly consider communication skills, adaptability, creativity, and problem-solving ability. In certain industries, demonstrated experience may be as important as formal certification.
However, this shift creates challenges. Without reliable assessment standards, it can be difficult to distinguish genuine expertise from superficial knowledge. Educational institutions therefore need to reconsider how they measure achievement without abandoning academic standards.
The future of education is unlikely to be determined by a choice between traditional institutions and digital alternatives. More plausibly, it will involve combining formal instruction, practical learning, and continuous professional development.
Questions
	•	Why has the traditional view of education been challenged?
	•	What does lifelong learning involve?
	•	How does education contribute to intellectual independence?
	•	Why are employers increasingly interested in skills beyond academic qualifications?
	•	What challenges arise when practical competence becomes more important in recruitment?
Reading 3: Climate Change and Collective Responsibility
Climate change is frequently discussed as an environmental problem, but its consequences extend far beyond the natural world. It affects economic stability, public health, international relations, food security, and patterns of human migration. Addressing it therefore requires a coordinated response involving governments, businesses, communities, and individuals.
One of the central difficulties is that responsibility for environmental damage is not distributed equally. Wealthier industrialized countries have historically contributed a substantial proportion of greenhouse gas emissions, while many developing nations are particularly vulnerable to extreme weather events despite having contributed relatively little to the problem.
This imbalance raises difficult questions about climate justice. Should countries that benefited from industrial development bear greater responsibility for financing environmental protection? Should developing economies be expected to limit emissions even when doing so could restrict their economic growth? These questions demonstrate why climate negotiations frequently involve complex political and economic disagreements.
Technological innovation is often presented as a potential solution. Renewable energy, improved energy storage, and more efficient transport systems can significantly reduce dependence on fossil fuels. However, technological progress alone is unlikely to be sufficient. Infrastructure investment, regulatory reform, and changes in consumption patterns are equally important.
Individual behavior also matters, although its influence should not be exaggerated. Choosing public transport, reducing food waste, and consuming fewer unnecessary products can contribute to broader environmental goals. Nevertheless, individuals cannot independently transform energy systems or introduce national environmental regulations.
Effective climate action consequently requires both personal responsibility and institutional accountability. Governments must establish meaningful policies, businesses must reduce harmful practices, and international institutions must encourage cooperation.
The challenge is not simply to acknowledge the seriousness of climate change but to reconcile environmental objectives with economic and social realities.
Questions
	•	Why does climate change affect more than the natural environment?
	•	What is meant by climate justice?
	•	Why can climate negotiations become politically complicated?
	•	Why is technological innovation insufficient on its own?
	•	How does the author distinguish individual responsibility from institutional accountability?
Reading 4: The Psychology of Success and Failure
Success is often presented as the direct consequence of determination, discipline, and personal ability. Popular narratives frequently celebrate individuals who overcome considerable obstacles through persistence. Although these qualities can contribute significantly to achievement, such accounts sometimes overlook the complex circumstances that influence people’s opportunities.
One important factor is access to resources. Individuals with financial security, supportive networks, and high-quality education may have advantages that are not immediately visible. Their achievements may reflect both personal effort and favorable circumstances. Conversely, talented individuals who experience economic hardship or social exclusion may encounter barriers that are difficult to overcome through motivation alone.
Another factor is the way people interpret failure. Some regard unsuccessful experiences as evidence of personal inadequacy, whereas others treat them as opportunities to reconsider their strategies. The latter approach can encourage resilience, particularly when individuals are able to identify specific mistakes and make meaningful adjustments.
However, the idea that every failure is beneficial should also be treated cautiously. Repeated setbacks without adequate support can damage confidence and discourage further attempts. Productive learning requires more than experiencing difficulties; it involves understanding their causes and identifying realistic ways forward.
There is also a distinction between persistence and stubbornness. Continuing to pursue a goal can demonstrate commitment, but refusing to reconsider an ineffective approach may waste valuable time and resources. Successful individuals are often those who can recognize when their original assumptions are no longer valid.
Ultimately, achievement is rarely attributable to a single quality. It emerges from the interaction of personal characteristics, external opportunities, social conditions, and the ability to adapt when circumstances change.
Questions
	•	Why does the author consider popular narratives about success incomplete?
	•	How can access to resources influence professional achievement?
	•	What distinguishes a productive response to failure from an unproductive one?
	•	Why is persistence not always beneficial?
	•	According to the text, what factors contribute to achievement?
Reading 5: Privacy in the Digital Age
The widespread collection of personal information has become an unavoidable feature of modern digital life. Online platforms, commercial organizations, and public institutions routinely gather data to provide services, improve products, and make decisions. Although these practices can offer considerable benefits, they also raise fundamental questions about privacy and individual autonomy.
Data collection can improve convenience in numerous ways. Navigation applications, for example, use location information to recommend efficient routes, while online retailers analyze purchasing behavior to suggest relevant products. In healthcare, the analysis of large datasets may help researchers identify patterns and improve medical treatment.
However, the same information can be used in ways that individuals neither anticipate nor fully understand. Personal data may be shared with third parties, used to create detailed behavioral profiles, or employed to determine which opportunities people are offered. Consequently, information collected for one purpose may eventually influence decisions in entirely different contexts.
A particularly concerning issue is the imbalance of power between individuals and organizations. Large technology companies often possess sophisticated systems for analyzing personal information, whereas users may have limited understanding of how their data is processed. Agreeing to lengthy privacy policies does not necessarily mean that individuals have given fully informed consent.
Regulation can help address these concerns, but legislation alone cannot guarantee responsible behavior. Organizations must establish transparent practices, minimize unnecessary data collection, and provide meaningful control over personal information.
Individuals also need greater digital literacy. Understanding privacy settings, recognizing suspicious requests, and questioning unnecessary permissions can reduce certain risks. Nevertheless, responsibility should not be transferred entirely to users.
A fair digital environment requires a balance between innovation, commercial interests, and fundamental rights. The central question is not whether personal data should ever be collected, but under what conditions such collection is legitimate.
Questions
	•	What are two potential benefits of personal data collection?
	•	How can information collected for one purpose affect people in other contexts?
	•	Why is informed consent difficult to achieve online?
	•	What responsibilities should digital organizations accept?
	•	What central question does the author raise about data collection?

sections.title: PART 4 — WRITING
sections.content:
At C1 level, writing should demonstrate a clear argument, sophisticated vocabulary, logical organization, precise grammar, and the ability to address complex issues from different perspectives.
Topic 1: Economic Growth Versus Environmental Protection
Task: Write an argumentative essay discussing whether economic development should take priority over environmental protection.
Consider:
	•	The economic importance of industrial development.
	•	The long-term consequences of environmental damage.
	•	The responsibility of governments and businesses.
	•	Whether sustainable development is a realistic objective.
Suggested length: 280–350 words.
Topic 2: Should Artificial Intelligence Replace Human Decision-Making?
Task: Discuss whether AI should be allowed to make important decisions in areas such as healthcare, education, employment, and law.
Consider:
	•	Efficiency and accuracy.
	•	Algorithmic bias and accountability.
	•	Human judgment and ethical considerations.
	•	The appropriate limits of automation.
Suggested length: 280–350 words.
Topic 3: The Declining Importance of Traditional Education
Task: Some people argue that traditional universities are becoming less relevant because information and professional training are increasingly accessible online. Discuss both perspectives and give your opinion.
Consider:
	•	Academic qualifications.
	•	Online education and independent learning.
	•	Practical experience.
	•	The social and intellectual value of universities.
Suggested length: 280–350 words.
Topic 4: Is Freedom More Important Than Security?
Task: Discuss whether individuals should be willing to sacrifice some personal freedom in exchange for greater public security.
Consider:
	•	Government surveillance.
	•	Personal privacy.
	•	Public safety.
	•	Legal and ethical limitations.
Suggested length: 280–350 words.
Topic 5: The Influence of Culture on Individual Identity
Task: Explain how cultural background influences individual identity and whether globalization is weakening traditional cultural values.
Consider:
	•	Language and traditions.
	•	Family and social expectations.
	•	Global communication.
	•	Cultural diversity and personal identity.
Suggested length: 280–350 words.

c2.intro:
C2 is the highest CEFR proficiency level. It represents an exceptional command of English, allowing learners to understand virtually everything they hear or read, synthesize information from multiple sources, express themselves spontaneously and precisely, and distinguish subtle differences in meaning, tone, style, and register.
At this level, learning is no longer primarily about memorizing grammar rules. It is about mastering linguistic nuance, stylistic flexibility, rhetorical techniques, idiomatic expressions, and sophisticated communication.
This curriculum includes:
	•	25 advanced grammar and language mastery topics, with 5 exercises each
	•	50 C2 vocabulary words with definitions and examples
	•	5 demanding reading comprehension texts, each with 5 questions
	•	5 advanced writing assignments
	•	Academic, professional, and literary language practice
	•	A C2 self-assessment checklist
	•	An 8-week study plan
All materials are in English, without translations.

sections.title: PART 1 — GRAMMAR AND ADVANCED LANGUAGE MASTERY
sections.content:
1. Advanced Inversion and Emphasis
Exercise: Rewrite the sentences using the expressions provided.
	•	I had never encountered such an extraordinary situation. (Never)
	•	She understood the consequences only after the decision had been made. (Only after)
	•	The company rarely makes such significant investments. (Rarely)
	•	He didn’t realize how serious the situation was until he saw the evidence. (Not until)
	•	We should under no circumstances disclose this information. Rewrite the sentence beginning with: Under no circumstances…
2. Complex Conditional Inversion
Exercise: Rewrite the sentences without using “if”.
	•	If I had been informed earlier, I would have taken action.
	•	If you should encounter any difficulties, contact the support team.
	•	If the proposal were to be accepted, significant changes would follow.
	•	If they had considered the consequences, they might have acted differently.
	•	If it hadn’t been for her intervention, the negotiations would have failed.
3. Advanced Mixed and Implied Conditionals
Exercise: Complete the sentences using the correct forms.
	•	Had he been more cautious, he __________ (not/find) himself in this predicament.
	•	If I weren’t so inexperienced, I __________ (handle) the situation differently yesterday.
	•	But for their financial support, the project __________ (collapse).
	•	If she had pursued her original ambition, she __________ (be) a professor now.
	•	Without your assistance, I __________ (never/complete) the investigation.
4. Advanced Modal Expressions of Deduction and Probability
Exercise: Complete the sentences using an appropriate modal construction.
	•	The documents __________ have been deliberately altered; several details are inconsistent.
	•	She __________ have misunderstood the instructions, although this seems unlikely.
	•	They __________ have been aware of the consequences before approving the proposal.
	•	He __________ be telling the truth, but I would still like to verify his account.
	•	The results __________ have been significantly different had the conditions been more stable.
5. Modal Perfects and Subtle Differences in Meaning
Exercise: Rewrite or complete the sentences according to the instructions.
	•	It was unnecessary for you to attend the meeting, but you did. Use needn’t.
	•	It was a mistake not to consult a specialist. Use should.
	•	Perhaps they misunderstood our intentions. Use may.
	•	I am certain she didn’t receive the message. Use can’t.
	•	It was possible for him to prevent the misunderstanding, but he failed to do so. Use could.
6. Advanced Passive Structures
Exercise: Rewrite the sentences in the passive voice.
	•	Investigators believe that the company deliberately concealed the evidence.
	•	Someone should have brought the discrepancy to the committee’s attention.
	•	The authorities are believed to have underestimated the potential consequences.
	•	They will have completed the negotiations by the end of the month.
	•	People consider his contribution to be particularly significant.
7. Passive Infinitives and Gerunds
Exercise: Complete the sentences using the appropriate passive form.
	•	She dislikes __________ (criticize) in public.
	•	The documents need __________ (revise) before publication.
	•	He claims __________ (misunderstand) by his colleagues.
	•	The proposal deserves __________ (consider) more carefully.
	•	The company appears __________ (investigate) by the authorities.
8. Advanced Causative Structures
Exercise: Complete the sentences using the correct forms.
	•	The director had the entire department __________ (reorganize).
	•	She got her research findings __________ (verify) independently.
	•	He had his reputation __________ (damage) by the scandal.
	•	We need to have the contract __________ (review) by a legal expert.
	•	The manager got the employees __________ (participate) in the training programme.
9. Advanced Reported Speech and Reporting Verbs
Exercise: Rewrite the sentences using the reporting verbs in brackets.
	•	“I didn’t authorize the transaction,” she said. (deny)
	•	“You should have informed me earlier,” he said. (reproach)
	•	“I will take full responsibility,” the director said. (undertake)
	•	“You must not discuss this matter publicly,” the lawyer said. (warn)
	•	“Perhaps we should reconsider our approach,” she said. (suggest)
10. The Subjunctive in Formal and Academic English
Exercise: Complete the sentences using the correct verb forms.
	•	It is imperative that every applicant __________ (provide) accurate information.
	•	The committee recommended that the proposal __________ (be) reconsidered.
	•	The regulations require that all documents __________ (submit) before the deadline.
	•	The director insisted that the investigation __________ (remain) independent.
	•	It is essential that no confidential information __________ (disclose).
11. Cleft Sentences and Advanced Information Structure
Exercise: Rewrite the sentences using the indicated structures.
	•	The lack of transparency caused the disagreement. Begin with: What…
	•	I object to the way the decision was made. Begin with: It is…
	•	She discovered the discrepancy, not her assistant. Begin with: It was…
	•	We need a more comprehensive solution. Begin with: The thing…
	•	The problem was not the cost but the lack of preparation. Begin with: What…
12. Advanced Participle and Reduced Clauses
Exercise: Rewrite the sentences using participle constructions.
	•	Because he had been informed of the risks, he decided not to proceed.
	•	The proposal, which was submitted at the last minute, was rejected.
	•	Although she was fully aware of the implications, she continued with the plan.
	•	After the negotiations had been concluded, both parties issued a statement.
	•	The individuals who were affected by the decision requested further clarification.
13. Absolute Constructions and Detached Structures
Exercise: Combine the sentences using absolute constructions.
	•	The evidence was insufficient. The committee postponed its decision.
	•	The negotiations were complete. The representatives left the building.
	•	The weather was exceptionally poor. The organizers cancelled the event.
	•	The documents having been reviewed, the director signed the agreement. Rewrite this using a different suitable structure.
	•	There being no reasonable alternative, we agreed to proceed.
14. Advanced Ellipsis and Substitution
Exercise: Rewrite the sentences to avoid unnecessary repetition.
	•	She understands the theory, but I do not understand the theory.
	•	Some researchers support the proposal, while other researchers oppose the proposal.
	•	He promised to attend the conference, and he attended the conference.
	•	I would have accepted the invitation if I had been able to accept the invitation.
	•	The first proposal was rejected, but the second proposal was not rejected.
15. Nominalization and Academic Style
Exercise: Rewrite the sentences using nominalization.
	•	The government decided to introduce stricter regulations.
	•	Researchers discovered that the results were inaccurate.
	•	The company failed to comply with the requirements.
	•	The committee rejected the proposal because it was financially impractical.
	•	The organization expanded its operations internationally.
16. Advanced Hedging and Qualification
Exercise: Rewrite the statements to make them more cautious and academically appropriate.
	•	This theory explains every aspect of human behavior.
	•	The new policy will definitely reduce unemployment.
	•	The results prove that the treatment is effective.
	•	Everyone agrees that technology improves education.
	•	This approach is the only possible solution.
17. Advanced Concession and Concessive Clauses
Exercise: Rewrite the sentences using the expressions provided.
	•	Although the evidence was limited, the researchers reached a conclusion. (Limited as…)
	•	Even though he had considerable experience, he struggled with the assignment. (Experienced though…)
	•	The proposal was expensive, but it was ultimately worthwhile. (Costly notwithstanding…)
	•	Despite the substantial investment, the project failed. (Much as…)
	•	Although the results were encouraging, further research was required. (Encouraging though…)
18. Advanced Prepositions and Complex Collocations
Exercise: Complete the sentences with the correct prepositions.
	•	The decision was made __________ the absence of sufficient evidence.
	•	His argument is difficult to reconcile __________ the available data.
	•	The organization is accountable __________ its shareholders.
	•	The findings are at odds __________ the previous research.
	•	The policy is conducive __________ long-term economic stability.
19. Advanced Determiners and Quantification
Exercise: Complete the sentences using the most appropriate expressions.
	•	__________ little evidence there was proved insufficient to support the claim.
	•	__________ of the two alternatives appears particularly convincing.
	•	There is __________ more to this issue than initially meets the eye.
	•	__________ the information available to us is reliable.
	•	__________ person involved was required to provide an explanation.
20. Advanced Comparison and Degree
Exercise: Complete the sentences.
	•	The more carefully the evidence is examined, __________ (apparent) the inconsistencies become.
	•	The situation was __________ (far/complex) than anyone had anticipated.
	•	No sooner had the negotiations begun __________ they encountered difficulties.
	•	The results were not so much unexpected __________ difficult to interpret.
	•	The proposal was all the __________ (convincing) because it addressed the main concerns.
21. Advanced Discourse Markers and Rhetorical Connectors
Exercise: Complete the sentences with appropriate expressions.
	•	The initial findings were encouraging. __________, the sample was too small to support a definitive conclusion.
	•	The policy is economically attractive. __________, its social implications remain uncertain.
	•	The organization has introduced stricter controls. __________, several weaknesses remain unresolved.
	•	__________ the substantial financial investment, the project failed to achieve its objectives.
	•	The theory is widely accepted. __________, a number of researchers have challenged its underlying assumptions.
22. Advanced Semantic Precision: Near-Synonyms
Exercise: Choose the most appropriate word.
	•	The decision had a __________ effect on the organization’s reputation. (profound / deep)
	•	The researcher attempted to __________ the validity of the findings. (establish / settle)
	•	The evidence was insufficient to __________ the allegation. (substantiate / suggest)
	•	The new policy may __________ existing inequalities. (exacerbate / intensify)
	•	The manager’s response was deliberately __________. (ambiguous / vague)
23. Idiomatic Language and Fixed Expressions
Exercise: Complete the expressions.
	•	The company has finally decided to __________ the bullet and restructure its operations.
	•	His explanation does not hold __________ under closer examination.
	•	The investigation brought several irregularities to __________.
	•	She has a tendency to take criticism with a grain of __________.
	•	The negotiations reached a __________ end after both parties refused to compromise.
24. Register, Tone and Stylistic Transformation
Exercise: Rewrite each sentence in the specified register.
	•	“The company made a terrible mistake.” Rewrite in formal academic language.
	•	“We need to sort this problem out immediately.” Rewrite in professional business English.
	•	“The results are pretty surprising.” Rewrite in precise academic language.
	•	“I don’t think this idea is going to work.” Rewrite as a diplomatic professional disagreement.
	•	“The whole thing was a complete disaster.” Rewrite in neutral analytical language.
25. Ambiguity, Implication and Pragmatic Meaning
Exercise: Interpret or rewrite the sentences.
	•	Explain the possible implied meaning of: “That is certainly an interesting interpretation.”
	•	Rewrite “You could have mentioned that earlier” to express stronger criticism.
	•	Explain the difference in implication between “I didn’t say he stole the money” and “I didn’t say he stole the money.”
	•	Rewrite the following sentence to eliminate ambiguity: “The manager discussed the proposal with the employee who was concerned.”
	•	Explain why the sentence “I suppose that might be acceptable” can communicate hesitation rather than agreement.

sections.title: PART 2 — C2 VOCABULARY
sections.content:
These 50 words are selected to develop precision, academic expression, critical analysis, and advanced professional communication.
No.	Word	Part of speech	Meaning and example
1	Abstruse	Adjective	Difficult to understand. The article explores an abstruse philosophical problem.
2	Acquiesce	Verb	To accept something reluctantly without protest. He eventually acquiesced to their demands.
3	Adroit	Adjective	Skillful and clever. She handled the negotiations with adroit diplomacy.
4	Ameliorate	Verb	To improve a difficult situation. The reforms were intended to ameliorate working conditions.
5	Anachronistic	Adjective	Belonging to an earlier period and seeming outdated. The regulation appears increasingly anachronistic.
6	Antithetical	Adjective	Directly opposed to something. Their approach is antithetical to democratic principles.
7	Assiduous	Adjective	Showing persistent care and effort. Her assiduous research produced impressive results.
8	Austere	Adjective	Severe, simple, or without unnecessary comfort. The building has an austere architectural style.
9	Belie	Verb	To give a false impression of something. His calm expression belied his anxiety.
10	Capricious	Adjective	Changing unpredictably. The market is affected by capricious investor behavior.
11	Circumspect	Adjective	Careful to avoid risks. The committee adopted a circumspect approach.
12	Cogent	Adjective	Clear, logical, and convincing. She presented a cogent argument.
13	Concomitant	Adjective/Noun	Naturally accompanying something. Economic growth often brings concomitant social changes.
14	Contingent	Adjective	Dependent on particular circumstances. Approval is contingent upon further review.
15	Deleterious	Adjective	Causing harm. The policy may have deleterious consequences.
16	Demur	Verb	To express disagreement or hesitation. Several members demurred at the proposed changes.
17	Derivative	Adjective	Lacking originality; based on something else. The film was criticized for its derivative storyline.
18	Dichotomy	Noun	A division between two contrasting things. The article challenges the traditional dichotomy between nature and culture.
19	Diffident	Adjective	Lacking confidence. Despite his expertise, he remained diffident in public.
20	Disparate	Adjective	Fundamentally different or unrelated. The study combines disparate sources of evidence.
21	Eclectic	Adjective	Drawing from a wide range of sources. Her writing reflects an eclectic range of influences.
22	Elucidate	Verb	To make something clearer. The professor attempted to elucidate the underlying principle.
23	Ephemeral	Adjective	Lasting for a very short time. The popularity of online trends is often ephemeral.
24	Equivocal	Adjective	Ambiguous or deliberately unclear. His response was notably equivocal.
25	Esoteric	Adjective	Understood by only a small group of people. The lecture contained several esoteric references.
26	Exigent	Adjective	Requiring immediate attention. The organization faced an exigent situation.
27	Extrapolate	Verb	To estimate or infer from existing information. Researchers extrapolated future trends from historical data.
28	Fastidious	Adjective	Extremely attentive to detail. She is fastidious about grammatical accuracy.
29	Fervent	Adjective	Showing intense passion or enthusiasm. He was a fervent supporter of educational reform.
30	Hegemony	Noun	Dominance or leadership by one group or state. The country sought to maintain its regional hegemony.
31	Implacable	Adjective	Impossible to calm or satisfy. The organization faced implacable opposition.
32	Inchoate	Adjective	Not fully developed or clearly formed. The proposal was still in an inchoate state.
33	Intransigent	Adjective	Unwilling to change one’s position. The negotiations failed because both sides remained intransigent.
34	Laconic	Adjective	Using very few words. His laconic response surprised everyone.
35	Lucid	Adjective	Clear and easy to understand. The author provides a lucid explanation.
36	Magnanimous	Adjective	Generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival. She was magnanimous in victory.
37	Mendacious	Adjective	Dishonest or untruthful. The report was based on mendacious claims.
38	Mitigate	Verb	To make something less severe. The agreement may mitigate the economic consequences.
39	Obfuscate	Verb	To make something unclear or confusing. The statement appeared designed to obfuscate the issue.
40	Ostensible	Adjective	Appearing to be true but possibly not genuine. The ostensible purpose was to improve efficiency.
41	Pernicious	Adjective	Having a harmful effect, often gradually. The misinformation had a pernicious influence on public debate.
42	Perspicacious	Adjective	Showing exceptional insight and understanding. Her perspicacious analysis identified the central weakness.
43	Proclivity	Noun	A natural tendency toward something. He has a proclivity for analytical thinking.
44	Recalcitrant	Adjective	Resistant to authority or control. The organization struggled with recalcitrant employees.
45	Recondite	Adjective	Concerned with a specialized or little-known subject. The book discusses recondite aspects of linguistic theory.
46	Sagacious	Adjective	Wise and showing good judgment. The decision reflected sagacious leadership.
47	Sanguine	Adjective	Optimistic, especially in difficult circumstances. Despite the setbacks, she remained sanguine.
48	Scrupulous	Adjective	Extremely careful, honest, and principled. The researcher maintained scrupulous standards.
49	Ubiquitous	Adjective	Present or found everywhere. Smartphones have become ubiquitous.
50	Vicissitude	Noun	An unexpected change in circumstances. The company survived numerous economic vicissitudes.

sections.title: PART 3 — C2 READING COMPREHENSION
sections.content:
These texts require more than identifying facts. You should interpret the author’s intentions, recognize implicit assumptions, evaluate arguments, and distinguish subtle shades of meaning.
Reading 1: The Limits of Human Rationality
Human beings have long regarded rationality as one of the defining characteristics of their species. The ability to evaluate evidence, anticipate consequences, and revise beliefs in response to new information is frequently presented as the foundation of intellectual progress. Yet research in psychology, economics, and neuroscience suggests that human reasoning is considerably less consistent than traditional accounts might imply.
People rarely approach decisions with complete neutrality. Prior experiences, emotional commitments, social identities, and cultural assumptions all influence the way information is interpreted. Even individuals who consider themselves exceptionally analytical may selectively attend to evidence that reinforces their existing convictions.
One particularly persistent phenomenon is confirmation bias. Rather than evaluating competing explanations impartially, individuals may scrutinize opposing arguments more critically while accepting supportive claims with comparatively little examination. The resulting asymmetry can create an illusion of intellectual certainty without necessarily improving the reliability of one’s conclusions.
Nevertheless, it would be simplistic to regard cognitive biases as evidence that rational thinking is fundamentally unattainable. Mental shortcuts can be useful, particularly when decisions must be made under conditions of uncertainty or time pressure. The problem arises when these shortcuts are applied indiscriminately to situations requiring careful analysis.
A more sophisticated understanding of rationality therefore involves recognizing its limitations. Intellectual maturity is not demonstrated by an unwavering belief in one’s own objectivity, but by a willingness to question one’s assumptions, acknowledge uncertainty, and revise conclusions when presented with compelling evidence.
Ultimately, the capacity for rational thought may depend less on eliminating every cognitive bias than on developing methods of identifying and mitigating their influence.
Questions
	•	Why does the author challenge traditional assumptions about human rationality?
	•	How does confirmation bias create an illusion of intellectual certainty?
	•	Why does the author reject the idea that cognitive biases make rational thinking impossible?
	•	What distinction does the author make between intellectual maturity and confidence?
	•	What does the final paragraph suggest about the most realistic approach to rational decision-making?
Reading 2: The Illusion of Meritocracy
Meritocracy is based on the appealing proposition that individuals should advance according to their abilities, achievements, and efforts rather than their social background or inherited status. As a political and social ideal, it promises a system in which opportunities are distributed fairly and personal accomplishment determines success.
However, the apparent simplicity of this principle conceals several difficulties. The first concerns the definition of merit itself. Academic qualifications, professional performance, creativity, leadership, and social contribution are not always easily measured. When institutions rely on narrow indicators of achievement, they risk rewarding those who perform well according to established criteria rather than those who possess the greatest potential.
A second difficulty concerns the distribution of opportunities. Individuals do not begin their lives with equivalent access to education, financial resources, social networks, or stable living conditions. Consequently, two equally talented people may encounter substantially different obstacles. Treating their eventual outcomes as purely individual achievements or failures ignores the structural circumstances that helped shape them.
There is also a psychological dimension to the problem. People who succeed within competitive systems may come to regard their accomplishments as entirely self-generated. This can encourage complacency and diminish their awareness of the support and opportunities they have received. Conversely, those who struggle may internalize their disadvantages as evidence of personal inadequacy.
None of this necessarily means that merit should be disregarded. Competence and achievement remain relevant considerations when allocating responsibility and opportunity. The more fundamental question is whether institutions can evaluate merit without reproducing the inequalities they claim to overcome.
A credible meritocratic system would therefore require more than competitive selection. It would also require meaningful access to education, transparent assessment, and a willingness to recognize the influence of circumstances beyond individual control.
Questions
	•	What is the central promise of meritocracy?
	•	Why can narrow definitions of merit produce unfair outcomes?
	•	How do unequal starting conditions complicate the assessment of individual achievement?
	•	What psychological consequences can result from interpreting success and failure as entirely personal?
	•	Does the author reject meritocracy, or argue for reforming it? Support your answer with evidence from the text.
Reading 3: Language, Power and the Construction of Reality
Language is often understood as a neutral instrument through which people communicate information about the world. Yet its role extends beyond the transmission of facts. The words individuals choose can influence how events are interpreted, which perspectives are considered legitimate, and which aspects of reality receive public attention.
Political communication provides a particularly clear illustration of this phenomenon. The same economic measure may be described as a necessary reform, an austerity programme, or an attack on public services. Each expression highlights a different dimension of the policy and encourages a particular interpretation. Although none of these descriptions is necessarily false, their rhetorical implications are not identical.
This does not mean that language can arbitrarily transform reality. Material conditions, historical events, and observable evidence impose limits on what can reasonably be claimed. Nevertheless, the vocabulary used to describe these conditions can shape public understanding and influence collective responses.
The relationship between language and power is especially significant when certain groups possess greater opportunities to establish dominant narratives. Governments, media organizations, academic institutions, and commercial interests can all influence which descriptions become widely accepted. Alternative interpretations may be marginalized, not necessarily because they lack credibility, but because they receive less institutional support.
Critical language awareness therefore involves more than identifying obviously misleading statements. It requires examining the assumptions embedded in apparently neutral expressions, considering what has been omitted, and asking whose interests a particular framing may serve.
Ultimately, language does not simply reflect the world. It also participates in the social processes through which meaning, legitimacy, and authority are negotiated.
Questions
	•	Why does the author reject the idea that language is merely a neutral communication tool?
	•	How can different descriptions of the same economic policy influence public interpretation?
	•	Does the author suggest that language can change material reality without limits? Explain.
	•	Which institutions may influence dominant public narratives?
	•	What does critical language awareness involve according to the text?
Reading 4: The Ethics of Scientific Progress
Scientific advancement is frequently regarded as an inherently positive process. New discoveries expand human knowledge, create technological possibilities, and offer potential solutions to longstanding problems. However, the assumption that every scientific development should automatically be pursued overlooks the ethical questions that arise when new capabilities have consequences extending beyond the laboratory.
Consider developments in genetic engineering. Advances in biotechnology may allow researchers to treat inherited diseases, improve agricultural productivity, and reduce certain health risks. At the same time, some applications could raise concerns about unequal access, unintended biological consequences, and the possibility of using scientific knowledge for discriminatory purposes.
The difficulty lies partly in distinguishing between what is technically feasible and what is ethically justifiable. Scientific research can establish whether a particular intervention is possible, but it cannot independently determine whether that intervention should be implemented. Such judgments require consideration of social values, individual rights, potential harms, and the distribution of benefits.
There is also a danger in imposing restrictions so broadly that potentially beneficial research becomes impossible. Excessively cautious regulation may delay treatments or prevent discoveries that could improve millions of lives. Conversely, inadequate oversight may permit irreversible consequences before society has properly evaluated the risks.
A defensible approach must therefore avoid both technological absolutism and indiscriminate prohibition. It should establish proportionate safeguards, encourage transparent debate, and involve a sufficiently diverse range of perspectives.
Scientific responsibility does not require researchers to abandon curiosity or innovation. Rather, it requires them to recognize that the ability to produce a result does not automatically confer the moral authority to do so.
Questions
	•	Why does the author question the assumption that scientific advancement is always positive?
	•	What ethical concerns are associated with genetic engineering?
	•	What is the difference between technical feasibility and ethical justification?
	•	Why can both excessive regulation and insufficient oversight be problematic?
	•	What principle does the author propose as the foundation of responsible scientific progress?
Reading 5: The Nature of Cultural Identity in a Globalized World
Cultural identity is often described as a relatively stable collection of traditions, values, beliefs, and practices inherited through family and community. Yet this description may underestimate the extent to which identity changes through migration, education, communication, and interaction with different societies.
Globalization has accelerated these processes. Digital platforms expose individuals to languages, cultural products, and political ideas that may be very different from those encountered in their immediate surroundings. International migration also creates communities in which multiple cultural traditions coexist and influence one another.
Some commentators regard these developments as a threat to cultural continuity. They argue that dominant global languages, commercial entertainment, and standardized consumer habits may gradually displace local traditions. There is evidence that certain cultural practices become less common when younger generations increasingly identify with international lifestyles.
However, cultural change should not automatically be interpreted as cultural disappearance. Traditions have never existed in complete isolation. Throughout history, societies have borrowed, adapted, and reinterpreted elements of other cultures. What appears to be a loss of authenticity may sometimes represent the emergence of new cultural forms.
Furthermore, individuals are not passive recipients of cultural influence. They select, reinterpret, and sometimes reject aspects of the traditions with which they are associated. A person may maintain a strong connection to their heritage while simultaneously adopting values and practices from other societies.
The more useful distinction, therefore, may not be between cultural preservation and cultural change, but between voluntary cultural adaptation and the imposition of dominant cultural norms.
A genuinely pluralistic society should allow traditions to evolve without requiring communities to abandon their distinctive identities. Cultural diversity is most likely to flourish when interaction takes place under conditions of mutual respect rather than unequal cultural power.
Questions
	•	Why might traditional descriptions of cultural identity be incomplete?
	•	What concerns do critics of globalization express?
	•	Why does the author argue that cultural change does not necessarily mean cultural disappearance?
	•	How does the text describe individuals as active participants in cultural identity?
	•	What distinction does the author make between cultural adaptation and cultural domination?

sections.title: PART 4 — ADVANCED WRITING
sections.content:
At C2, you should be able to produce texts with sophisticated argumentation, stylistic control, nuanced vocabulary, and precise organization.
Topic 1: The Limits of Freedom in Modern Society
Task: Write an argumentative essay examining whether individual freedom should have limits in a modern democratic society.
Address:
	•	Freedom of expression.
	•	Public safety and social responsibility.
	•	Government regulation.
	•	The relationship between individual rights and collective interests.
Suggested length: 350–450 words.
Topic 2: Is Objective Truth Possible?
Task: Discuss whether objective truth can exist independently of personal beliefs, cultural assumptions, and social influences.
Address:
	•	Scientific evidence.
	•	Subjective interpretation.
	•	The influence of language and culture.
	•	The difference between facts and opinions.
Suggested length: 350–450 words.
Topic 3: The Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
Task: Examine the ethical implications of allowing artificial intelligence to make decisions that directly affect human lives.
Address:
	•	Accountability.
	•	Algorithmic bias.
	•	Human autonomy.
	•	Economic and social consequences.
	•	Possible regulatory approaches.
Suggested length: 350–450 words.
Topic 4: Has Modern Society Become Too Dependent on Convenience?
Task: Discuss whether the pursuit of convenience has weakened people’s independence, patience, and ability to deal with difficulties.
Address:
	•	Digital technology.
	•	Consumer culture.
	•	Personal development.
	•	The relationship between convenience and quality of life.
Suggested length: 350–450 words.
Topic 5: The Meaning of Progress
Task: Evaluate whether technological and economic development should be considered sufficient evidence of societal progress.
Address:
	•	Economic prosperity.
	•	Social equality.
	•	Environmental sustainability.
	•	Cultural development.
	•	Human well-being.
Suggested length: 350–450 words.
